header.title: Testimonia Divinae Scripturae Et Patrum (Incertus): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Isidorus Hispalensis
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1435.tmp1435.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1435.tmp1435.opp-lat: Ch. I: 'immediator' (marked sic) read as 'unus mediator'. Ch. II: the Johannine Comma appears in an unusual form, with 'in Christo Jesu' attached to the earthly witnesses. Ch. III: Jeremiah 'in toto proderunt vobis' lacks the negative the sense requires ('non proderunt'); [not] supplied. 'multi sunt per eam' read as 'multi [ambulant/intrant] per eam'. Ch. V: 'nam qui adit munera acceptio. I-lis, vivet' is corrupt; read as 'qui odit munerum acceptiones vivet'. 'qui arguunt meliora sperabunt' follows the Latin of Prov. 24:25 loosely. The Leviticus citation is actually Deuteronomic (Deut. 27:19). Ch. VII: 'plaga dolosi dividit vulnera' rendered literally (cf. Sir. 27:28). 'in hujus' read as 'in his'. The Proverbs verse ends 'ut avertat iram suam ab eo' as in the source. The Exodus attribution of 'Obey your parents' is the compiler's (cf. Col. 3:20). Ch. IX: 'qui exaltamur' read as 'qui exaltantur'; 'Viro cupido tenaci ... et homini libido' follows Sir. 14:3 imperfectly ('homini livido', envious man, is likely meant). Several book attributions ('Ecclesiastes' for Ecclesiasticus/Sirach, etc.) are kept as given.

Book attributions are often loose (e.g. 'Ecclesiastes' for Ecclesiasticus/Sirach, 'Leviticus' for Sirach 23, 'Proverbs' for Sirach). CAP. XI: 'adjiciet te' (to a just man) is odd; rendered literally ('add to you'), perhaps for 'adjiciet [accipere]'. 'apostareadeo (sic)' read as 'apostatare a Deo'. 'dictas (sic)' read as 'dici' (Prov. 25:7, 'to be told to come up'). CAP. XII: 'est (sic) in ea ossibus' is corrupt; a word or phrase seems lost ('[...]'). 'non agnoscimur' is odd (perhaps for 'non agnoscitur', 'it is not recognised'); translated as printed. 'Metior' read as 'Melior', 'forns' as 'fortis'. CAP. XIV: 'habeat caput (sic)' rendered literally. CAP. XV: Sirach 23:10 supplies 'interrogatus' (questioned), implied in the text; 'non velle' read as imperative 'noli velle'. CAP. XVI: 'sensum interitum (sic)' read as 'sensus, interitum'.

'Ecclesiastes' citations in this collection are mostly from Ecclesiasticus (Sirach); kept as the text gives them. Ch. XVII: 'Psalmo CIXXIV' read as CXXXIX (Ps. 139:12 Vulg.); 'Multum' read with the editor's 'mutum'. 'Noli tacitus esse' likely corrupt for 'noli citatus esse' (Sir. 4:34, 'do not be hasty'). Ch. XVIII: 'inficias' read as 'in phialas'; 'pilo' read as 'pilo' (pestle, after Prov. 23:31 LXX/Vet. Lat.), uncertain; 'infirmibus' read with editor as 'infimis'; 'ebriositatis animos tas' is garbled, rendered tentatively; 'efficatione' read as 'efficacia', 'in Ecclesiasticis' cites Eccles. 7:3; 'quantum est unius panis' rendered loosely; 'sanguine' (Sir. 9:13 'spiritu tuo') kept. Ch. XIX: 'in zelo' probably 'in zelum mittit inimici' (makes the enemy jealous); rendered literally. Ch. XXI: heading reads 'De volo', taken as 'De voto'; 'in vultu oblectabitur' rendered after Eccl. 7:4 ('corrigitur'), tentatively; 'propter delaturam' read as 'propter delaturam' (slander), uncertain. Ch. XXII: 'petitur' read as 'partitur'; 'diligentia ossibus' probably corrupt for 'irrigatio'; in 1 Thess. 4:8 'hominem' after 'spernit' is printed but the sense requires 'he who despises [this]'.

Several citations are misattributed in the collection itself (e.g. 'Ecclesiastes' for Ecclesiasticus/Sirach, 'Proverbs' for Sirach, 'Romans' for 1 Corinthians 9:27, 'Isaiah' for Ezekiel 13:3-4 in places); translated as given. XXIII: 'in pluribus ejus non erit cur' read as 'non eris curiosus' (Sir 3:22). XXIV: 'baptizatur a mortuo' rendered by sense (Sir 34:30). XXVI: 'Qui minoratur cute' read as 'corde'; 'Compedes. Iedes' read as 'compedes in pedibus'; 'scientia non tenebit domos' obscure, rendered by sense (Sir 21:17); 'Qui ducat fatuum sapientis' read as 'docet fatuum'. XXVII: 'exhorruit litem' read as 'exaccendit' (kindles). XXVIII: 'Qui allati facit' read as 'altam'; 'extus (sic)' read as 'ex his'; 'eorrogatione' read as 'consolatione'; 'Item illic. In Proverbiis' appears doubled in the source; the phrase 'Lucerna est mandatum legis' seems displaced from another citation.

Ch. XXX: 'nil' read as 'Nilus' (the Nile). Ch. XXXI: 'in noctibus' read as 'innocentibus'; 'ad hoc perducuntur ut videantur' is incomplete, and '[to have been wronged]' is supplied conjecturally; 'Sermones subtiles magis (sic) quam facito' is corrupt, and the end of the clause cannot be recovered; 'dum alia malis vincuntur ab illo mala' is unclear, rendered as 'others are overcome by evils, evils by him'; 'timendum' read as 'timidum'. Ch. XXXII: 'leguntur' read as 'teguntur'; the shadow/image/truth sentence is garbled and is rendered literally; 'Nullum propterea honores...' is apparently missing a negative ('[dis]honour'); 'ventii' read as 'ventri'. Ch. XXXIII: 'Ad fac eui publicam patienter jam fugiunt' read as 'ad faciem publicam patientiam fingunt'; 'nec increpatio (sic)' is taken as 'neither the rebuke [nor]...', with a verb supplied; 'pio sua increpatione' is corrupt, and '[weakness]' is a conjecture; 'Securus quippe malina' is corrupt (perhaps 'militat'), so the sense of that sentence is uncertain; 'adnusceatur' read as 'admisceatur'; 'dentque' read as 'denique'.

Text is heavily corrupted by scanning; several readings are conjectural. 'non vclare' read as 'non vigilare' (or perhaps 'non velle'); sense unclear. 'qualis sine timore sapientiæ' and the sentence ending 'surrexit credentem' are marked (sic) and defective. 'bonus, etiam si regnet, servus est' appears inverted; translated as the familiar Augustinian 'etiam si serviat, liber/regnat'—literal text reads 'a good man, even if he reigns, is a slave'. 'Prima mors... nh miraque parte' read as 'ex utraque parte'. 'fit deterior magis quam facis' read as 'fit de te magis quam facis'. 'Virgo lidei' read as 'regula fidei'. 'carena o' read as 'carendo'; 'non bene admittitur' read 'nunquam male admittitur' is uncertain. 'non is homo' read as 'non nisi homo'. 'Labor piorum... nascendo, non ascendendo' rendered as printed.

nodes.text: APPENDIX XI.
TESTIMONIES OF DIVINE SCRIPTURE AND OF THE FATHERS.
CHAPTER ONE. — On the one God.

1. In the Prophet. Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one, and you shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength. In the Gospel. No one is good but God alone. Paul to Timothy. For there is one God, and [one] mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for us.
CHAP. II. — On the distinction of the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

1. In the Epistle of John. For there are three who give testimony on earth, the Spirit, the water, and the Blood; and the three are one in Christ Jesus; and there are three who bear testimony in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and the three are one. In the Second Epistle. For many deceivers have gone out into this world, who do not confess that our Lord Jesus has come in the flesh; these are deceivers, and they are antichrists.
CHAP. III. — On conversion and contempt of the world.

1. In Solomon. Do not be slow to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath comes suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you. In the Gospel. Therefore I say to you: every sin and blasphemy is forgiven to men. Whoever blasphemes against the Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in the one to come. In Proverbs. Far better is bread with sweetness in peace than a house full of many goods, with wicked rivalries and strife. In the same. He who conceals an injury seeks friendship. He who hates to conceal separates friends and household. In the same. Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent. If you approach them, they will seize you, like the teeth of a lion in devouring. In Jeremiah. Correct your ways and your thoughts. Do not trust in false words, for they will [not] profit you at all. In the Gospel. Enter through the narrow gate, for wide and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many go by it. How narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it. In the same. For as in the days of Noah, so too will be the coming of the Son of Man; as they were in those days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and they did not perceive until the flood came and took them all, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
CHAP. IV. — On the fear of the Lord.

1. In Proverbs. The fear of the Lord will add days; but the years of the wicked will perish. In the same. The fear of the Lord is the stronghold of the just, but ruin to those who do evil. In the same. Blessed is he who is wary of all things through fear, for he who is hard of heart falls into evils. In Ecclesiastes. The fear of the Lord drives out sin, for he who is without fear cannot be justified. In the same. [It is] the fear of the Lord not to despise a just man who is poor, and not to justify a sinful man who is rich. In Proverbs. If you do not hold fast to the fear of God earnestly, your house will quickly be overthrown. In the same. The fear of the Lord hates malice, and pride, and the ways of the wicked. That God knows the secrets of the heart. In every place the eyes of the Lord watch the good and the wicked. In the same. Death and the underworld are laid open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of men? In the Acts of the Apostles. You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show us which one of these two you have chosen.
CHAP. V. — That one must judge justly.

1. In Exodus. You shall not pervert the judgement of the poor in judgement, and you shall not kill the just. Again there. You shall not show partiality, nor accept gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and take away the just word. In Proverbs. He who accepts gifts destroys himself; but he who hates the acceptance of gifts will live. Again there. He who says the just man is wicked will be cursed by peoples and hateful to nations, but those who reprove will hope for better things. Again there. Open your mouth to the word of the Lord, and judge all with integrity. Open your mouth and judge justly; and distinguish between the poor and the weak. In Leviticus. Cursed is he who perverts the judgement of the stranger, and the orphan, and the widow, and all the people say: So be it, so be it. In Ecclesiasticus. Presents and gifts blind the eyes of judges; and like one who is mute in the eyes of many, it turns away correction. In Job. For the testimony of the wicked is death; and fire will burn up the houses of those who accept gifts.
CHAP. VI. — That one must do good to the poor.

1. In Proverbs. He who insults the poor sins; but he who has mercy on the poor is blessed. He who wrongs the poor provokes him who made him, but he who honours him has mercy on the poor. He who gives to the poor will not be in want, but he who turns away his eye will be in great need. In Leviticus. You shall not finish reaping the harvest of your field, and what falls from your harvest you shall not gather, nor shall you gather in your vineyard the grapes falling from the clusters, but you shall leave them for the poor and the strangers. For I am the Lord your God. In Proverbs. He who stops his ears so as not to hear the weak, he too will call upon the Lord, and there will be no one to hear him. In Job. Let not the pleasure of your soul turn away from the prayers of the weak, when they are in need.
CHAP. VII. — That one must not walk in deceit.

1. In Ecclesiastes. Woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to the sinner who walks on two ways. Again there. A heart that walks on two ways will have no success, and the perverse of heart will stumble in them. He who throws a stone on high, it falls on himself; and the blow of the deceitful divides wounds; and he who digs a pit falls into it; and he who sets a snare for his neighbour will perish in it; the worst deed rolls back upon him who does it, and he will not know whence it comes to him. In Job. Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the wrath of God. In Jeremiah. Their tongue is a wounding sword, the words of their mouth are deceitful; speaking peaceably to his neighbour, and holding enmity within himself; shall I not then visit [punishment] on these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a people? In the Gospel. Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves; by their fruits you will know them. In Proverbs. If your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and do not exult at his overthrow, lest perhaps the Lord see, and it displease him, so that he turn away his wrath from him. Paul the Apostle. If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink, for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head; and God will repay you. In the Gospel. Peter came to Jesus and said to him: Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Seven times? The Lord answered: I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven. In Exodus. Obey your parents in all things; for this is pleasing to God.
CHAP. VIII. — On the proud son.

1. In Proverbs. There will be nothing good for the deceitful son; he who does not honour his father and drives away his mother, the son will be put to shame and will be a reproach. Again there. The son who abandons his father's instruction will ponder words of malice. Again there. For him who curses father and mother the light will be extinguished; and the pupils of his eyes will see darkness. Again there. He who, angering his father or his mother, thinks he does not sin, is like a wicked man. Again there. The blessing of the father strengthens the houses of the sons, but the curse of the mother uproots the foundations.
CHAP. IX. — On treasure.

1. In Proverbs. Better is a small portion with the fear of the Lord than great treasures without fear; better is a small gain with justice than many fruits with iniquity. Again there. A good name is better than great riches; good favour is above gold and silver. In Ecclesiastes. Nothing is more wicked than to love money; for such a man sells even his own soul, since in his life he has cast away his inmost parts. For a greedy, tight-fisted man wealth is not good, nor for a man [given to] lust; to what purpose is gold? As he came out of his mother's womb, naked he returns, as he came, and he will take nothing from his labour to carry away in his hand. I said, a stillborn child is better than he; there is more rest for it than for them. In Zephaniah. All who exalt themselves in silver and gold have perished; I will pour out their blood like mud, and their flesh like the dung of oxen; and silver and gold will not be able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath. In Habakkuk. O he who acquires evil greed for his house; you have devised shame for your house, your soul has sinned. In Ecclesiastes. The way of sinners is full of stumbling-blocks; at their end are the underworld, and darkness, and punishments.
CHAP. X. — On almsgiving.

1. In Proverbs. Do not say to the poor man: Go, and come [back], tomorrow I will give, when you can do good at once, for you do not know what may happen on the following day. Again there. He who has pity on the poor man is blessed; almsgiving and faith cleanse sins; and he who shows pity obtains mercy. He who honours God has pity on the poor man. In the Gospel. Give back to the Almighty, and do not turn away from him who wishes to receive much. Again there. But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. Again there. Nevertheless give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you. Again there. And Jesus, looking intently, saw the rich who were putting their gifts into the treasury, and he saw also a certain poor widow putting in two copper coins, [and] he said: Truly I say to you that this poor widow has put in more than all, for all these put in out of their abundance into the gifts of God; but she, out of what she lacks, has put in all the living that she had. In Proverbs. As silver is tested in the furnace, and gold, so are chosen hearts with the Lord. Again there. The furnace tests the potter's vessel, and temptation and tribulations [test] just men.
CHAP. XI. — On reproof and on pride.

1. In Proverbs. Reprove a wise man, and he will love you; [reprove] a fool, and he will go on to hate you. Again. Give a wise man an occasion, and he will be wiser; make [it] known to a just man, and he will add to you. He who loves instruction loves understanding, but he who hates the one who reproves him is foolish. Again. The undisciplined man does not love the one who reproves him, and he does not converse with the wise. Again. He who has received instruction will be among good things, and he who keeps rebukes will become wise. Again there. When a pestilent man is chastised, the fool will become more shrewd; but if you reprove a prudent man, he understands the meaning; if you flog a fool in the middle of the council, doing him insult, you do not take away his folly. In Ecclesiastes. He who hates reproof is the track of a sinner; and those who fear the Lord will turn to their heart. In Proverbs. As a dog returns to its vomit and becomes hateful, so is a fool who has turned back in his malice to his sins. In Ecclesiastes. The beginning of pride is for men to fall away from God, since pride is the beginning of all sin. Again there. At two things my heart was afraid, and at the third anger came upon me: a warrior failing through want, and a sensible man despised, and he who passes over from justice into sin—God prepares him for the sword. In the Psalms. He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house. In the Apostle. God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud. In Proverbs. He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress, but he who is insolent of lips will terrify himself. Again there. The Lord will destroy the houses of the proud; everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before the Lord. Again there. The proud son has evil eyes; the rash man is lifted up by his eyelids, and the proud man is called a pestilence. Again there. Do not be proud before the face of the king, nor take your stand in the places of the powerful. It is better for you to be told [to come up] than to be humbled in the sight of a powerful man. In Ecclesiastes. Pride is hateful before God and men. Again there. And why are you proud, earth and ashes? Again there. He who touches pitch will be defiled by it; he who associates with a proud man puts on pride. Again there. Those who are proud will be crushed by insult and will be humbled, and the lofty will fall by the sword. Again there. Pride has ceased, and the riches of the proud, because what is lofty among men is an abomination before God.
CHAP. XII. — On gentleness, on patience and on humility.

1. In Proverbs. A gentle man is the physician of the heart; [...] an understanding heart [is] in the bones. Again there. Better is a gentle man with humility than he who divides spoil with the insolent. In Ecclesiastes. Be gentle in hearing a word, so that you may understand, and with wisdom bring forth a true answer. Again there. Son, accomplish your works in gentleness, and you will be loved by men. Again. Patience will be found in the heart of a good man; but in the heart of fools we are not recognised. In Proverbs. A patient man is better than a strong one, and he who holds back his anger is better than he who takes a city. Again. He who refrains from uttering a harsh word is prudent; and a patient man is abundant in wisdom; but the faint-hearted man is exceedingly foolish. Again. Every work of the humble man is manifest before God, but the wicked will perish in the day of evils. Again there. A humble answer turns away anger. And again in Isaiah. To whom shall I look, says the Lord, but to the humble, and the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? In the Gospel. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. In the Epistle of James. Humble yourselves before the face of the Lord, and he will exalt you.
CHAP. XIII. — On wisdom.

1. In Proverbs. The wise will possess glory, and the foolish share out disgrace. Again there. Wisdom is an ornament for the young, and grey hairs are the glory of the old. Again there. The heart of the wise will possess understanding. Again there. Better is a wise man than a strong one, and a man who has prudence than a great field. Again there. Happy the wise man who in his wisdom will meditate on truth and justice; in his understanding he has pondered the circumspection of God. Again there. A wise man will keep silent until the [right] time; but the wanton and imprudent will not observe the time. Again there. The wise man makes himself agreeable in words. Again there. The devout man remains in wisdom like the sun; but the fool will change like the moon. Again there. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools in the house of luxury. Again there. An experienced man has taught many, and is pleasant to his own soul. In Job. For wisdom is to fear the Lord, and to keep oneself from evil knowledge.
CHAP. XIV. — On the conduct of the young.

1. In Ecclesiastes. Son, from your youth receive teaching, and up to [old] age you will find wisdom. Again there. Son, in your youth test your soul, and if it is wicked, do not give it power. For not every kind [of thing] pleases every soul. Again there. Young man, speak in your own cause, so that when you are questioned your answer may have a head. In many things be as one ignorant, and at the same time inquiring; in the midst of great men do not presume to speak, and where there are elders, do not speak much; lightning goes before hail, and favour goes before a modest man.
CHAP. XV. — One must not swear, and must not speak falsely, and must not lie.

1. In Leviticus. Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, for there are many falls in it, and do not mix in names, since you will be diminished by them; for as a servant constantly [questioned] is not free from bruises, so everyone who swears and names [God] will not be cleansed from all sin. Again. A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house, and if he swears in vain, he will not be justified. In the Gospel. You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not swear falsely, but shall render your oaths to the Lord? But I say to you not to swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no. What is more than this is from evil. In Proverbs. The unjust witness brings in falsehoods, and will send judgements upon brothers. Again there. A hasty witness will have an unjust tongue. Again there. A faithful witness will deliver a soul from evils; but the deceitful man kindles falsehoods. Again there. A changeable man falls into evils with his tongue; a false witness will not go unpunished; he who accuses unjustly does not escape. Again there. A lying witness will perish, but an obedient man speaks cautiously. Again there. A club, and a sword, and an arrow are deadly; so too is a foolish man who bears false witness against his friend. Again there. A lying tongue hates the truth, and an unrestrained mouth makes strife. In Wisdom. The mouth that lies kills the soul. Do not be willing to tell any lie, for the habit of it is not good. Again there. Better is a poor man walking in truth than a rich liar. In Jeremiah. No lie is of the truth. In the Psalm. You will destroy those who speak a lie.
CHAP. XVI. — One must not commit fornication.

1. In Proverbs. A woman captures the precious souls of men. Will anyone bind fire in his bosom and not burn his clothes? Or will he walk on coals of fire and not burn his feet? Again there. The adulterer, through lack of understanding, brings about the destruction of his soul; he gains pains and disgraces; and his reproach will not be blotted out. An unjust thought is an abomination to the Lord, but the words of the holy are chaste. Again there. The father of a man who loves wisdom will rejoice; but he who feeds harlots will lose his wealth. In Ecclesiastes. Do not give your soul over to fornication in this, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance. Again. Wine and women make the wise fall away, and put the sensible to reproach; and he who joins himself to fornicators will be wicked; rot and worms will inherit him. In the Gospel. Everyone who looks at a woman so as to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart. Again there. Everyone who puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery; and he who marries a woman put away by her husband commits adultery. In Exodus. And you shall make them linen breeches, to cover the shame of the body from the loins to the knees.
CHAP. XVII. — Again, on restraint of the mouth.

1. In Proverbs. Strife stirs up hatred, but friendship protects all who do not quarrel. Paul to Timothy. But avoid profane novelties of words, for they advance greatly towards impiety, and their speech creeps like a cancer. In Psalm 139. A talkative man will not be directed upon the earth. In Proverbs. In much speaking you will not escape sin; but he who spares his lips will be wise. Again there. He who uses many words harms his soul. Again there. Making yourself silent, you will seem to be wise. Again there. He who answers a word before he hears, it is folly and reproach to him. Again there. Death and life are in the hands of the tongue; but he who is restrained will eat its fruits. Again there. He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distresses. Again there. If you see a man hasty in words, know that a fool has more hope than he. Again there. Do not be silent with your tongue, and useless and slack in your works. Again there. He who is a whisperer in all things, and not needed, will be hated. Again there. The silent and sensible man will be honoured with honour. Again there. In the midst of the sensible keep a word for its time. But in the midst of those who deliberate be constant. Again there. Do not accustom your mouth to undisciplined speech, for in it is a word of sin.
CHAP. XVIII. — Drunkenness is to be fled.

1. In Proverbs. Wine is a wanton thing, and drunkenness insolent; and every fool is mingled with these. Again there. Do not be a wine-bibber, nor stretch yourself out to pamper the flesh; for every drunkard and fornicator will beg, and will be clothed in torn rags, and every sluggard. Again there. For if you give your eyes to bowls and cups, at the last you will walk more naked than a pestle. Again there. Let rulers who are prone to anger not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom, and cannot judge rightly for the weak. Again there. Thorns grow in the hands of a drunkard. In Ecclesiastes. Wine and women make the wise fall away, and put the sensible to reproach; and he who joins himself to fornicators will be wicked; rot and worms will inherit him. Again there. A drunken and straying woman [is] great anger, and insult, and her shame is not covered. Again there. For a disciplined man a little wine [is enough], and in sleeping he will not be troubled by it, and will not feel the pain of wakefulness. Again there. Do not challenge those who love wine, for wine has destroyed many. As fire tests hard iron, so wine will expose the hearts of the proud; wine is equal to life for men, [taken] without drunkenness. Wine was created for gladness, not for drunkenness; from the beginning, wine drunk in moderation [is] the exultation of the soul and heart. Wine drunk in excess causes provocation, and anger, and many ruins, [through] the spirits of drunkenness. In Ecclesiastes. It is best to go into the house of mourning rather than into the house of drinking. Paul to the Ephesians. Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit. Again to the Corinthians. Neither drunkards nor revilers will possess the kingdom of God. In Proverbs. Do not attend to the deceit of a harlot woman, who for a time fattens your throat; yet at the last you will find [her] more bitter than gall, and sharper than a two-edged sword. Again there. Do not be too much with another's woman, nor be joined in the embraces of one who is not yours. Again there. Son, do not let desire for beauty overcome you, nor be captured by your eyes, nor be carried off by your eyelids; what is the price of a harlot but that of one loaf? Again there. As the moth [destroys] a garment, and the worm wood, so a wicked woman will destroy a man. Again there. Do not look upon a woman of many desires, lest you fall into her snares. Do not keep company with a dancing-girl, nor listen to her, lest you perish by her charms. Again there. Do not give a woman power over your soul, lest she tread upon your strength and you be confounded. Do not give your soul to fornicators in anything, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance. Do not wander in the vices of the city, nor roam in its streets; turn your face away from an adorned woman, and do not look upon another's beauty. Every woman for hire is trodden down like dung in the road. Many who admired the beauty of another's wife have been rejected. For her conversation burns like fire. Do not recline on a couch with another's wife, and do not dispute with her over wine, lest your heart incline towards her, and through blood you slip into perdition.
CHAP. XIX. — Small children who lack knowledge are to be corrected.

1. In Proverbs. He who spares the rod hates his son; he who loves [him] instructs [him] diligently. Again there. Disgrace is not hidden in an uninstructed son. Again there. Do not cease to correct a small child, for if you strike him with the rod he will not die; you indeed will strike him with the rod, but you will deliver his soul from death. Again there. Instruct your son, and he will gladden you, and will give grace to your soul. Again there. A young man who is with the holy, his way is straight; the ear hears, the eye sees, and both are works of the Lord. In Ecclesiastes. Have you sons? Instruct them from their boyhood. Have you daughters? Guard their body, and do not show them a cheerful face. Again there. He who loves his son is constant with the lash for him, that he may rejoice in him at his end, and not grope at the doors of neighbours; he who teaches his son will be praised in him, and will be honoured because of him among friends. Again there. He who teaches his son with zeal provokes the enemy; the father has died, and is as though not dead, for he leaves one like himself behind him. Again there. An unbroken horse runs into thorn-bushes; a son left to himself runs headlong. Bend his neck in youth, and beat his sides while he is a child, lest he grow up and become stubborn and not obey you, and be a grief to your soul. In Ecclesiastes. Be constant with a holy man, whomever you know to keep the fear of God; as far as you can, beware of your neighbour, and deal with the wise and sensible.
CHAP. XX. — Just measures and weights.

1. In Deuteronomy. There shall not be in your house a weight great and small; there shall not be in your house a measure great and small; but let your weight and measure be just, that you may be of many days upon the land which the Lord your God will give you as your lot, for everyone who does unjust things is abominable to the Lord. In Proverbs. A false balance is an abomination before the Lord; but a just weight is acceptable to him. Again there. A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful balance is not good before him.
CHAP. XXI. — On a vow.

1. Again there. As soon as you have vowed a vow to the Lord, you shall not delay to pay it; so pay what you have vowed; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. In Ecclesiastes. A fool raises his voice in laughter; but a wise man will scarcely laugh quietly. Again there. Indignation is better than laughter, for by [a sad] face [the heart] will be bettered; the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of the foolish in the house of pleasure. In Deuteronomy. A man's things shall not be upon a woman, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord. Again there. Parents shall not die for children, and children shall not die for parents; but each shall die in his own sin. Paul to the Ephesians. And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and reproof of the Lord. In the prophet Hosea. Sow justice for yourselves, and gather the vintage of the fruit of life; seek out for yourselves the light of justice; wait for the Lord until he comes to you; gather the vintage of the fruits of his justice. In Proverbs. Who will boast that he has a clean heart, or who will dare to say that he is pure from sins? Again there. Son, shed tears over your dead, and begin to lament as one who has suffered grievously, and cover his body according to custom, and do not neglect his burial; because of slander, weep bitterly the mourning for him for one day, and be comforted because of sadness.
CHAP. XXII. — One must not defraud; and on not boasting.

1. In Exodus. You shall not commit theft, and you shall not lie. In Proverbs. He who shares with a thief hates his own soul. Paul to the Corinthians. Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. In Proverbs. Trust in the Lord with your whole heart, but do not be lifted up in your own wisdom. Again there. Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord and turn aside from evil; then there will be health for your body and care for your bones. Again there. I have seen a man who thought himself wise; but a fool had more hope than he. In Isaiah. Woe to those who are wise in themselves and prudent in their own sight. Paul to the Romans. For claiming to be wise, they become fools. To the Corinthians. Where is the wise man, where is the scribe, where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? Again there. Let no one deceive himself. If anyone seems to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written: I will catch the wise in their cunning; and again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. In Ecclesiastes. It is better for you to be told, Come up to me, than to be humbled in the sight of the powerful. In Exodus. For your murmuring is not against us, but against God. Paul to the Thessalonians. He who despises, despises not man but God. To the Romans. For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one many are made just.
CHAP. XXIII. — Not to search into higher things, nor to listen to heretics.

1. In Proverbs. He who trusts in falsehood feeds on the winds; he himself chases flying birds; for he abandons the way of his own vineyard and wanders from the tracks of his own field's tillage; he walks through dry places and deserts and land set in drought, and gathers barrenness with his hands. Again there. Withdraw, then, from another's water, and do not drink from another's spring, that you may live a long time, and years of life will be added to you. Again there. He who pursues vain things lacks sense. Do not add to his commands, lest you be reproved and be a liar. In Ecclesiastes. Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger [than you], but always think on what the Lord commands you; and in his many works do not be curious; for suspicion has led many astray, and has held their minds in vanity. In the book of Wisdom. We hardly guess at the things that are on earth, and find with labour the things that are before us; but who has searched out the things that are in the heavens? And who knows your mind, unless you give the judgement?
CHAP. XXIV. — On fasting.

1. In Ecclesiastes. He who is washed after [touching] a dead body, what has his washing profited him? So too the man who fasts for his sins and does the same things again. What has he profited by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer? A saving sacrifice is to heed the commandments and to depart from all iniquity. In the Gospel. When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men as fasting. Amen I say to you, they have received their reward; but you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not be seen by men as fasting, but by your Father, who sees in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
CHAP. XXV. — The example of the ant or the bee for man, of labour without sloth.

1. In Proverbs. Go to the ant, O sluggard, and seeing its ways, imitate them and be wiser than it. For though it owns no field, has no one driving it, and is under no master, how it prepares its food in summer! And it makes an abundant store at harvest. Or go to the bee, and learn how industrious it is, and what holy work it carries on. Its labours kings and common people use for health; it is beloved by all and glorious; and though weak in strength, it has been brought forth proclaiming wisdom. How long will you lie, sluggard? When will you rise? You sleep a little, you sit a little. You doze a little, you fold your hands on your breast a little. Then poverty will come upon you like an evil traveller, and want, like a good runner, will flee from you. Again there. A sluggard, when rebuked, does not blush. So too those who barter grain at harvest. Again there. Desires kill the sluggard, for his hands do not resolve to do anything. Again. The sluggard seeks excuses and says: There is a lion in the streets, and in the streets murderers. Again there. As a door turns on its hinge, so the sluggard on his bed. Again there. The sluggard seems to himself wiser than one who brings a message to the multitude.
CHAP. XXVI. — On the fool.

1. A foolish man contrives evils for himself, and stores up fire in his lips. Faithful lips do not befit a fool, nor lying lips a just man. Again there. Why have riches in abundance for the fool, when the senseless cannot possess wisdom? Again. A foolish son is anger to his father and grief to his mother. Again there. He who lacks sense does not desire wisdom; rather it is called imprudence. Again there. The mouth of a foolish man is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul. Again there. A stone is heavy and sand hard to carry, but a fool's anger is heavier than both. Again there. As a dog that returns to its vomit and becomes hateful, so is a fool who in his malice has turned back to his sins. Again there. He who is lacking in heart thinks empty things, and an imprudent and erring man thinks foolish things. The heart of a fool is like a broken vessel, and will hold no knowledge at all. To a fool wisdom is shut up, and the knowledge of the sensible man is words to be declared. Teaching is fetters on the feet of fools, and like chains on the right hand; the fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely smile quietly. Again there. The heart of fools is in their mouth, and the mouth of the wise is in their heart. He who teaches a fool is like one who glues together a potsherd. Again there. Sand and salt and a lump of iron are easier to carry than an imprudent man and an impious fool. Again there. Do not even take counsel with fools, for they cannot keep [a secret]. Again in the prophet Isaiah. The fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vain things.
CHAP. XXVII. — Anger is to be put away.

1. In Proverbs. Every simple soul is blessed, but a passionate or angry man does not act honourably. Again there. The fool declares his anger the same day, but the shrewd man hides an insult. Again there. There are those who wound with speech like swords. The angry man acts without counsel, but the prudent man endures much. Anger destroys even the wise, but a humble answer turns away anger. Again. An angry man stirs up quarrels, but a patient man calms even those to come. Again. Do not be a friend to a passionate man. Do not stay with an angry friend, lest you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul; the fool pours out all his anger, but the wise man dispenses it in portions. Again. A passionate man digs up strife, and an angry man has swallowed down sins. In Ecclesiastes. The angry man kindles strife, and the sinful man disturbs friends, and casts slander among those who have peace. Again there. Jealousy and anger shorten one's days, and anxiety brings on old age before its time. Again there. Do not be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools. Paul to the Ephesians. Now put away all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, much talking. In the Gospel. Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgement. Again. Whoever says to his brother *raca* [empty-head] will be liable to the council; and whoever says “fool” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.
CHAP. XXVIII. — Here, miscellaneous [texts].

1. In Ecclesiastes. Be gentle in hearing a word, so that you may understand, and give answer with wisdom. In Proverbs. A prudent servant will prevail over the folly of his masters, and will divide a share among brothers. Again there. A deceitful son will have nothing good, but a wise servant's doings will prosper. In Ecclesiastes. If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul, and treat him as a brother, because you acquired him with the blood of your soul. If you harm him unjustly, and he takes himself off and departs, whom will you seek, and by what road will you seek him? Again there. In Proverbs. The commandment of the law is a lamp; as an unripe grape is harmful to the teeth, and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practise it. Again there. A man kills himself by his own malice. Again there. By what things a man sins, by these he is also tormented. Again there. The Lord made man and left him in his own free choice; he added commandments and precepts, if he is willing to keep the commandments and to keep pleasing faith; he set before you water and fire: stretch out your hand to whichever you wish; before man are life and death, good and evil; whatever pleases him will be given him. Again there. As the moth [harms] a garment and the worm wood, so sadness harms the heart. Again. A glad heart makes good will; but in a sad man the bones dry up. In Jeremiah. Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man, and makes flesh his arm's strength, and whose heart has turned away from the Lord. Again there. Those who trust in man are cursed, for God made him nothing. In Ecclesiastes. Do not fail those who weep in consolation, and walk with those who mourn; do not be slow to visit the sick, for by this you will be made firm in love. Paul to the Romans. I bruise my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself become reprobate. In Proverbs. The Lord will destroy the houses of the proud. Again there. He who builds his house high seeks ruin. Again there. By wisdom a house will be built, and by understanding it is raised up; by sense storehouses are filled, full of all good and precious things. Again there. Do not bring every man into your house; for the snares of the deceitful are many. In the Canticles. Beware of the little foxes that destroy [the vines]. The same. Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and see nothing at all, like foxes in the desert. In the Gospel. Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours. Again there. Whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery. Again there. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns to you, saying: I repent, forgive him. Again there. He who sows the good seed is the Son of man, and the field is this world; the good seed are the sons of the kingdom. But the tares are the sons of the wicked one; the enemy who sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age; and the reapers are the angels. Just as, then, the tares are gathered and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age. In Solomon. There are six things which the Lord hates, and a seventh which his soul detests: a haughty eye, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising most wicked thoughts, feet swift to run into evil, one who utters a lie, a false witness, and him who sows discord among brothers.
CHAP. XXIX. — Testimonies of the Fathers.

1. There are four disturbances of the human soul, that is, desire, joy, fear and sorrow. The mind itself is memory, and the power which is called memory. Again there. There are eight principal vices which assail the human race. The first is *gastrimargia*, which is gluttony of the belly; the second fornication; the third *philargyria*, that is, avarice, or love of money; the fourth anger; the fifth sorrow; the sixth *acidia*, that is, anxiety, or weariness of heart; the seventh *cenodoxia*, that is, boasting, or vainglory; the eighth pride (in the book of the Conferences, namely of Cassian).
CHAP. XXX. — Testimonies from the Sentences of Evagrius to the Brothers.

1. For just as a flame burns up a forest, so hunger extinguishes evil visions. Again there. A sleepy monk falls into evils, but he who keeps watch will be like a sparrow. Again there. As fire melts wax, so good wakefulness [melts] the worst thoughts. There. He who loves silver will not see knowledge, and he who gathers it will be darkened. There. As fire tests gold and silver, so temptation [tests] the heart of a monk. Again there. Better is poverty with knowledge than riches with ignorance. There. As a raven flies out of its nest, so an unclean soul out of its body. There. As the south-west wind on the sea, so rage from the heart of a man. Again there. Better is a layman serving a brother in sickness than a monk who has no pity on his neighbour. A sluggard monk grumbles much, and a sleepy one complains of a pain in his head. A double-tongued monk throws the brothers into confusion, but a faithful one brings rest. Better is a gentle layman than an angry or passionate monk. God loves a gentle monk, but drives a turbulent one away from himself. Humility goes before charity, and love before knowledge. For as the morning star in the sky, and as the Nile in paradise, so is a pure mind in a gentle soul. For him who seeks out banquets the light is extinguished, and his soul will see darkness. Set your bread by weight, and drink your water by measure, and the spirit of fornication will flee from you. Give wine to the elders, and bring food to the sick, because they wore down their flesh in their youth. I have seen an angry old man, exalted in his time, but a young man had more hope than he. He who loves the bee eats its comb, and he who gathers it will be filled with honey.
CHAP. XXXI. — Testimonies from the book of Saint Martin, not that bishop of Tours, but this one was a father of monks.

1. However weak someone is, if you praise him at once he will be stronger. If you show admiration for one carrying a small weight, he gives way. If you tell a sluggard that he is swift, he will at once fly. Although this stain of pride assails many generally, yet it is to be feared by none more than by those who [advance] either spiritually towards the perfection of virtues or carnally towards an abundance of vices. Where the height of honour is greater, there the wind of exaltation is always stronger. We believe easily, and we grow angry before we are judged; for many are driven by suspicions and, interpreting the worse from another's face and laughter, grow angry with the innocent. The curious man who inquires what has been said about him, and digs out malicious talk even if it was spoken in secret, disquiets himself; for while they interpret, they are brought to the point that they seem [to have been wronged]. [The wise man] passes over many injuries, and most he does not receive, because either he does not know of them, or, if he knows, he turns them into play and jest. If the one who did the injury is a good man, do not repay it; if a bad man, do not imitate him; yield to the wiser, forgive the fool. Everyone has within himself the mind of a king, so that he wants licence to be given to him against others, but not to others against himself. It is not fitting that one who sins should correct sins: for if the wise man were to be as angry as the indignity of crimes demands, he would not have to be angry, but to go mad. Nothing is more glorious than to exchange anger for friendship. Is someone angry? Challenge him in return with kindness, and the enmity falls at once. The remedies of physicians help not in the onsets of illnesses but in their remissions. For often a lie keeps the face of truth. Often a lie is hidden under the appearance of truth. For just as a flatterer sometimes shows the face of a friend, and a pleasant one, so [falsehood] is coloured with likelihood. Praise sparingly, blame more sparingly; for excessive praise is as blameworthy as immoderate censure. The prudent man never feeds his mind on idleness; sometimes he has [leisure], yet never slackness. The virtue of humility is sought not in loftiness of words but in purity of mind. Abstain also from base words, for licence in them nourishes shamelessness. Make your speech subtle rather than [...]. You will make all men your equals if you do not despise inferiors through pride, and do not fear superiors through living rightly. Be kind to all, a flatterer to none; familiar with few, yet fair to all. To one who is eager for wisdom and teachable, impart what you know without arrogance when he asks; what you do not know, ask to have imparted to you without concealing your ignorance. The just man does not betray secrets, for he keeps silent what is to be kept silent and speaks what is to be spoken; and so he has deep peace and secure tranquillity, while others are overcome by evils, but evils by him. Magnanimity is to be neither a fearful man nor a rash one.
CHAP. XXXII. — From the book of Saint Ambrose.

1. In the vine let religion, in the oil peace, in the rose the modesty of sacred virginity take root. My brother is white and ruddy: white deservedly, because [he is] the splendour of the Father; ruddy, because he is the offspring of a virgin; the colour of both natures shines and glows in him. Chastity even makes angels: he who has kept it is an angel; he who has lost it, a devil. A virgin is she who marries God; a harlot, she who makes gods. Hence the sons of Noah, walking backwards, covered his nakedness. What the impudent one saw, the modest one blushed at, the dutiful one covered, [the brothers] who would have been offended if they too had seen. How great is the power of wine, that wine should strip him whom the floods did not strip! For he who teaches ought to excel him who is taught. It is more tolerable to have a virgin mind than [a virgin] flesh. The shadow for the carnal Jews, the image for us, the truth for those who will rise again. For we know these three things to exist according to the law: shadow, image, truth; the shadow in the law, the image in the Gospel, the truth in the judgement; and therefore through Moses the law through the shadow, as through a man, the figure through the law, more truly through Jesus. What is the treasury? The consolation of the faithful, the support of the poor, the rest of the needy. Sins are either forgiven, or blotted out, or covered: forgiven through grace, blotted out through blood, covered through charity. When David says: Deliver me from blood, he asks to be delivered from mortal sins. Do not subject yourself to the powers of the flesh, you whom God willed to be free. You have no excuse from the pursuit of marriage; it belongs to pleasure, not to necessity. If you are kind towards the needy, you will be great before God. Since you call God Father, show this in your deeds. A good mind is a choir of God, an evil mind a choir of demons. As many vices as the soul has, so many masters [it has]. The foundation of piety is continence, and the summit of piety is friendship. Agree with no one who persuades you to do what is not good. It is worst for sinners to come together when they sin. Many foods hinder charity, and incontinence in food makes a man unclean. It is not the foods brought in through the mouth that defile a man, but what is brought forth from evil habits. Receive from God what you cannot receive from man. It is better to throw a stone in vain than a word. The wise man will be brief in his words in judgement; a long narration belongs to ignorance. When you are set over men, remember that you have God [over you], and when judging men, know that you too will be judged by God. Revere a wise man as an image of the living God. Do not [dis]honour anyone because he has no money; it is difficult for a rich man to be saved. You will never be wise if you think yourself wise. God does not hear the prayer of a man who does not hear the needy. He who does not obey a wise man will not obey God either. Do not take up what you did not lay down, but let what is yours suffice you. Flee drunkenness as disgraceful, for he who is [given] to the belly, like a beast, is overcome. If you labour as much for the soul as you labour for the body, you will be wise. Honour a philosopher, as a minister of God, next after God. To serve others is better than to be served by others. It is better to die of hunger than to stain the soul through incontinence of the belly. He who speaks a word about God to those to whom it is not permitted is to be thought a betrayer of God. It is not true that he worships God who harms a man. It is better to have nothing than, having much, to share with no one. If you do not give to the needy when you can, you will not receive from God when you ask.
CHAP. XXXIII. — Testimonies from the book of Prosper.

1. If my rusticity made me unfit, I believed I was made fit by the faith of you who commanded [me]. The treatment of necessary questions, even if it does not instruct the mind of the inquirer in what it seeks, exercises the mind of the seeker to [its] health. Knowledge, just as without the gift of God, which is charity, it puffs up, so, if charity is mixed with it, builds up. The just are separated from the wicked for ever in such a way that neither the rewarded end their reward nor the damned their punishment. For just as bodily fullness holds all who are full equally, although each has taken food not equally but according to capacity, so all the saints, even if they are distinguished by some difference of their degrees, will all be made perfect in one beatitude, because they will also be blessed in one perfection. And on the day of judgement it is not words that will be sought from us, but works. He who does not believe, by not having faith, will be able to have neither justice of heart nor salvation. The speech of a bishop ought to be so weighty that it shuts no one, however unskilled, out from understanding it. A sound mind ought to seek the fruit of obedience incorporeally more than to avoid the reproach of unjust disparagement. When truth has cried out from any quarter, let it be ascribed not to human ingenuity but to God. Grounded in the virtue of obedience and patience, they do not dispute the decrees of their elders, but carry them out. In public they now feign patience, and hide the poison of anger in the mind, ready to harm when they find a time for harming. So ought every man to be cared for, now by teaching, now by exhorting, now by bearing with, now by rebuking, that with the help of Christ no one in this life should despair of salvation. Reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and teaching, as if he said: reprove your equals, entreat your elders, rebuke the younger. One who is gently chastised shows reverence to the one who chastises, but one offended by the harshness of excessive rebuke [accepts] neither the rebuke nor salvation. Those who cannot be rebuked on account of their [weakness] are to be borne with gentle kindness. Just as virtue is burdensome to the vicious, so vicious pleasure is bitter to the friend of virtue. For as long as someone curiously considers the sins of others, so long does he not know his own sins, which he ought to know and weep over; but if, turned towards himself, he looks at his own conduct, he does not seek what to censure particularly in others, because he has in himself what to lament; therefore we ought not readily to accuse [the sins] of our brothers, but to groan [over them]. For those whose sins lie hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor published by others, if they refuse to confess or amend them, will have God, whom they have as witness, also as avenger. He is insulting who reproves falsely; and he reproves falsely who gives insult. [For] he who does not have heavenly things [in view] securely provides earthly things to those who fight vigorously. Those riches are to be sought by us which can both adorn and protect us; for this reason, therefore, [other riches] are to be fled by those who fight for God; those who wish with their whole heart to have such riches do not seek them without labour, do not find them without difficulty, do not keep them without care, do not possess them without anxious delight, do not lose them without grief. He who enjoys idle quiet, unless he lives spiritually, lives in the manner of cattle. No one possesses God except one who is possessed by God; let him first be God's possession, so that God may become his possession and portion. The Creator of all, to whom none of the things he made can be equalled, does not deign to be possessed together with the things he created. He who wishes to possess God, let him renounce the world, so that God may be his blessed possession. He does the work of God who does not abandon things consecrated to God, with the intention not of any greed but of most faithful stewardship. Therefore the possessions which priests receive when given up by the people are no longer to be thought things of the world, but of God. Adam and Eve did not blush because they were outwardly protected by a divine garment; indeed before sin they were naked and did not blush, because they had committed nothing against the will of God for which they should be put to shame. Open concupiscence would not, then, have moved those who had fallen from their Creator to the creature through desire for divinity, had not hidden pride first corrupted them. The concupiscence of the flesh was fulfilled by them in that they tasted of the forbidden tree; the concupiscence of the eyes, in that they desired their eyes to be opened; and the ambition of the world, in that they believed they could become what God is. For health becomes sweeter when pain tortures, and the bitterness of sickness commends the sweetness of lost health. Adam made us liable to all evils through his own fault, from which the coming of Christ freed us through grace. Any delicacies, if taken without desire, do no harm, and cheap foods, if taken greedily, often hinder progress in abstinence. Moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach; drunkenness weakens mind and body. They do nothing against abstinence who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body, and it is not pleasure that offers it to them but infirmity that permits it. For if I break my fast and refresh any who arrive, I not only fast but set an example of charity. But if for the sake of abstinence I sadden spiritual brothers, whom I know to be delighted by my relaxing, it is not to be called my abstinence but a vice. Just as virtue, if it is true, justifies the mind that truly clings to it, so, if feigned, it condemns it. The mind cannot have the kingdom of virtues unless it has first shaken off the yoke of vices. A just punishment gives the envious man as many torturers as the envied man has had praisers. Since excellence makes a man envied, envy will be the punishment of sin; nor can a remedy be applied by man to one whose wound is hidden. For each speaks of what he loves, and hears with delight what he turns over in constant thoughts. For it is thought which, if base, defiles the mind, and, if honourable, purifies it. Sordid thoughts do not make the mind sordid, but sordid thoughts arise from a sordid mind. For to chaste ears obscene words die away with the sound, and do not break into the secret place of a modest heart. Through the mouth of the flesh the delight of taste does not break into the mind; nor does base speech break out from the mind, unless the mind first willingly corrupts itself. Each man often has on his lips the same names whose desires he carries in a wounded heart, and the baseness which he is ashamed to practise in deed he holds guilty in his mind, not by human judgement but by divine. Consider, I beg, how the envious are to be punished by their own evils, whom even the good things of others punish. What does it profit anyone if outwardly, where he can be thought great, he shines, and inwardly, where God alone sees, he is foul?
CHAP. XXXIV. — On fasting

1. Fasts, abstinences, vigils, almsgivings, and other things of this kind ought to increase the good. For not to watch [is] sin (sic). Nothing keeps us so free from all sin as fear of punishment and the love of God. Those puffed up through the haughtiness of vain talk desire their words to be praised rather than done; nor are they concerned for holiness of deed, but for the elegance of laboured speech. For a man sins in that part in which he loves God less; and if we love Him with our whole heart, there will be nothing in us by which we may serve the desire of sin. As we wish to be helped, so let us help others according to our strength; or if the means is lacking, let us keep the will to help. If I see someone sinning, and not only do not rebuke him but even consent to the sinner, I make myself a sharer in his damnation, and I sin in all who sin, when through a certain malice of a cruel mind I do not reprove those whom I know to have sinned. He who loves a friend for the sake of some temporal advantage is shown to love not the friend but the advantage.
CHAP. XXXV. — From the book of Sentences.

1. True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another, and no one sins against another before he sins against himself. Men are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved, for it is one thing to love what they were made, another to hate what they do. The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of mouth and heart is one; but to speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself with one's own voice. He has a good understanding who rightly understands what is to be done, such as [is] without fear of wisdom (sic). A death is not to be thought bad which a good life has preceded. Whatever evils the Lord inflicts on the just through the wicked is not the punishment of a crime but the testing of virtue; for a good man, even if he is a slave, reigns. The proud devil led proud man to death; the humble Christ led obedient man back to life. For as the one, exalted, fell and cast down the one who consented, so the other, humbled, rose and [raised] the one who believed (sic). That hatred is perfect which lacks neither justice nor knowledge, that is, that you neither hate men because of their vices nor love vices because of men. They are in great want who are in iniquity, not having the work of justice and the treasures of wisdom; but those who serve the Lord acquire those goods which cannot perish. Confession of sin is good if healing follows it. For what does it profit to uncover a wound and not apply medicine? The first death holds the suffering soul in the body; on both sides it is held in common, so that the soul suffers from its own body what it does not wish. When you do good, do it cheerfully; for if you do any good sadly, it is done by you rather than you do it. For a humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good ones. No unjust man does well, even if what he does is good, for the spirit of fear profits nothing where there is not the spirit of charity. Fairness of mind is better than health of body. For Christ is the end of the law, by whom the law of justice is not taken away but fulfilled. As the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so man ought to await mercy and truth from God. The first salvation is to turn away from sin, the second is not to despair of pardon; for he perishes for ever who does not have recourse to the remedy of penance before a merciful judge. In the rule of Christian faith we are roused at three times: evening, morning, and midday; for in the evening the Lord [was] on the cross, in the morning in the resurrection, at midday in the ascension. The first pertains to the patience of the one slain, the second to the life of the one raised, the third to the glory of the majesty of the one seated at the right hand of the Father. Tribulations harass men to this end, that the vessels of election may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace. Better is the sadness of one repenting of iniquity than the gladness of one doing iniquity. It is good to be conquered by truth, so that for correction truth may overcome pleasure. For it overcomes even the unwilling. Those who worship idols are like those who see vain things in dreams. But if their souls awake, [each] understands by whom it was made, and does not worship what he himself made. Those who thirst for God ought to thirst with their whole substance, that is, both soul and flesh; for God gives his bread to the soul, that is, the word of truth, and God supplies the necessities of the flesh, for he feeds both, since he made both. Two loves make two cities in the whole world: the love of God makes Jerusalem, the love of the world Babylon. Let each one therefore question himself, and he will find of which he is a citizen. There is no difficulty in going without, except when there is desire in having; and therefore that alone is rightly loved which is never wrongly admitted. In the first man it was shown that man's choice availed for death, but in the second that God's help availed for life. For the first man was only man, but the second God and man; sin was committed by forsaking God, justice is not done without God. The Lord says: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; that is, through me one comes to me, in me one arrives, one abides in me. A good odour is a good reputation, which anyone will have by the works of a good life while he follows the footsteps of Christ: he pours, as it were, the odour of precious ointment over his feet. The toil of the godly is exercise, not condemnation. The just are born of God, not of men, since a man becomes just by being born [again], not by rising up, whence also the regenerate are called sons of God. It is one thing to move with the body, another to move with the heart: to move with the body, as the body changes place; to move with the heart, as you change the heart's affection. If you love one thing and used to love another, you are not where you were.
